mainTopic: רבה and רב חסדא on a ערל and the principle of הואיל, and a ברייתא comparing ערלה to טומאה in the קרבן פסח.
overview: The גמרא explains that רבה and רב חסדא disagree about the verse "לכפר עליו". The verse teaches that an offering atones for its owner and not for someone else (חבירו). רבה says a ערל is not eligible for כפרה, so having him in mind does not disqualify the קרבן פסח. רב חסדא says a ערל still counts, הואיל (since) he could circumcise himself. The גמרא then notes that in the case of baking on יום טוב for a weekday, the two seem to reverse their views on הואיל. רבה is reconciled: הואיל does not work when an action (מילה) is still missing. רב חסדא is reconciled: he uses הואיל only to be strict, not to be lenient. Next, מר זוטרא asks רבינא about a ברייתא that learns partial ערלה from partial טומאה. The גמרא works out whether that טומאה means impure meat or impure people, and gives two answers. It then starts a new challenge from another clause of the ברייתא, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The verse at the root of the dispute
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא names the verse that רבה and רב חסדא are arguing about: an offering atones "for him" and not for his fellow.
steps.simpleTranslation: They disagree about this verse: "And it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him." This means for him, and not for his fellow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is telling us that the earlier argument between רבה and רב חסדא really comes from how each of them reads one verse. It is setting up the next two steps, where each opinion is explained.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse teaches that a קרבן brings כפרה to its owner and not to someone else. This is why having another person in mind (שינוי בעלים) can be a problem. The open question is who counts as "his fellow" (חבירו).

keyTerms.meaning: "And it shall be accepted for him to atone for him" (ויקרא א:ד)
His fellow, meaning another person who is not the owner

steps.whyThisMatters: Both opinions agree on what the verse says. They only disagree about who fits into the category of "his fellow."

phrases.english: They disagree about this verse:
"And it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him" —
phrases.notes: This פסוק is from ויקרא א:ד.

phrases.english: for him, and not for his fellow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Grounds the earlier dispute (on the previous amud) in a verse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An offering atones for its owner and not for his fellow.

steps.title: רבה: the "fellow" must be someone who could get atonement
steps.stepSummary: רבה says "his fellow" must be like the owner, meaning a person eligible for כפרה. A ערל is not eligible, so he is excluded.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה holds that "his fellow" must be similar to him. Just as the owner is someone who can get atonement, so too the fellow must be someone who can get atonement. This excludes this uncircumcised man, who is not someone who can get atonement.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה explains his reading of the verse. The "other person" who causes a problem must be someone who could actually get כפרה from this קרבן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה compares the fellow to the owner (דומיא דידיה). A ערל may not eat or bring a קרבן פסח, so he cannot get כפרה from it. Having him in mind is therefore not a real change of owner, and the offering stays valid.

phrases.english: Rabba holds: his fellow must be similar to him.
Just as he is someone eligible for atonement —
so too his fellow must be eligible for atonement,
to exclude this uncircumcised man
who is not eligible for atonement.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבה's reading of the verse from step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only a person eligible for כפרה counts as "his fellow". A ערל is excluded, so intent for him does not disqualify the קרבן.

steps.title: רב חסדא: the uncircumcised man still counts, since he could fix himself
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says a ערל is obligated in the קרבן פסח, so he counts as eligible for כפרה, because he could circumcise himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא holds: this uncircumcised man too, since he is obligated, is someone eligible for atonement. This is because, if he wants, he can fix himself.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא gives the opposite reading. A ערל does count as a "fellow" who could get כפרה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא's reasoning is that the ערל is still under the obligation (בר חיובא). The only thing holding him back is something he could fix right now by having a מילה. This style of reasoning is called הואיל: "since he could, we treat him as if he does."

keyTerms.meaning: "Since": treating a possibility as if it were already real
Fix himself (here, by having a מילה)

steps.confusionAlert: Keep the word הואיל in mind. The next step attacks רב חסדא for using exactly this kind of reasoning.

phrases.english: And Rav Chisda holds:
this uncircumcised man too,
since he is someone obligated —
he is eligible for atonement,
since, if he wants, he can fix himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב חִסְדָּא סָבַר: הַאי עָרֵל נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite reading to רבה's in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ערל counts as eligible for כפרה because he could circumcise himself (הואיל). So intent for him does disqualify the קרבן.

steps.title: Does רב חסדא really accept "since"? The baking case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב חסדא: in the case of baking on יום טוב for a weekday, he says the baker gets מלקות, while רבה says he does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: But does רב חסדא accept the reasoning of "since"? Yet it was said: someone who bakes on יום טוב for a weekday — רב חסדא said he is lashed; רבה said he is not lashed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the explanation from step 3 by quoting a different argument between the same two אמוראים. In that argument, their positions seem reversed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 3, רב חסדא relied on הואיל. In the baking case he rules that the baker gets מלקות, which seems to mean he rejects הואיל. רבה, who did not use הואיל for the ערל, is lenient here. The next step spells out the reasoning.

keyTerms.meaning: One who bakes on יום טוב for a weekday

phrases.english: But does Rav Chisda accept "since"?
But it was said:
one who bakes on a Festival for a weekday,
Rav Chisda said: he is lashed.
Rabba said: he is not lashed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אִית לֵיהּ לְרַב חִסְדָּא הוֹאִיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning given for רב חסדא in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's use of הואיל to make the ערל count as בר כפרה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Contradiction with his own ruling elsewhere. In the baking case, רב חסדא gives מלקות, which implies he rejects הואיל.

steps.title: Spelling out the baking dispute: רבה uses "since", רב חסדא rejects it
steps.stepSummary: רבה exempts the baker: since guests might come and eat the food on יום טוב, the baking is treated as allowed. רב חסדא says we do not say הואיל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said he is not lashed because we say: "Since, if guests happen to come, the food is fit for him to use on יום טוב, now too it is fit for him." So he is not lashed. רב חסדא said he is lashed because we do not say "since."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reasoning behind each opinion in the baking case. This makes the contradiction clear: here רבה uses הואיל and רב חסדא rejects it, the opposite of what we just said about the ערל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Baking on יום טוב is allowed only for food eaten on יום טוב. רבה says the bread could be needed if guests show up, so the baking counts as permitted. רב חסדא refuses to count a possibility that did not actually happen. This contradicts step 3 for רב חסדא, and step 2 for רבה. Steps 6 and 8 answer this.

keyTerms.meaning: Guests happen to come to him

steps.whatToRemember: In the baking case, רבה uses הואיל and רב חסדא rejects it. In the ערל case, רב חסדא seemed to use הואיל and רבה did not. The גמרא must now explain why this is not a contradiction.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. In the baking case, הואיל leads to leniency (no מלקות). In the ערל case, הואיל leads to strictness (the קרבן is disqualified). Either way, the question is only whether each אמורא accepts הואיל consistently.

phrases.english: Rabba said he is not lashed:
we say: "Since, if guests happen to come to him,
it is fit for him,
now too it is fit for him"
and he is not lashed.
Rav Chisda said he is lashed:
we do not say "since."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה אָמַר אֵינוֹ לוֹקֶה: אָמְרִינַן הוֹאִיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the baking dispute quoted in step 4, completing the challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: The consistency of both רבה and רב חסדא with what they held in steps 2 and 3.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב חסדא explicitly rejects הואיל in the baking case, yet relied on it for the ערל. רבה accepts הואיל in the baking case, yet did not apply it to the ערל.

steps.title: רבה does not contradict himself
steps.stepSummary: רבה's two rulings fit together. In the פסח case the ערל still has to act (circumcise), while in the baking case the baker has nothing left to do.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is fine that רבה does not contradict himself. Here (the פסח) an action is missing. There (baking on יום טוב) no action is missing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רבה can use הואיל for the baker but not for the ערל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With baking, the guests could come right now, and the baker has nothing more to do, so הואיל works. The ערל would first have to circumcise himself, which is a missing action. So we do not treat him as already fit.

keyTerms.meaning: Lacking an action; something still needs to be done

phrases.english: Granted, Rabba against Rabba is not difficult:
here, an action is lacking,
phrases.notes: The ערל must still circumcise himself.

phrases.english: there, no action is lacking.
phrases.notes: That's the baking case, where guests could just show up.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction for רבה that was raised in steps 4-5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (מחוסר מעשה vs. not)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבה seems to use הואיל in one place and reject it in another.
steps.terutzMaskana: הואיל works only when no action is missing.

steps.title: But רב חסדא seems to contradict himself
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says a ערל counts because he could circumcise, which is a הואיל-style argument. Yet he rejects הואיל in the baking case.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רב חסדא against רב חסדא is difficult!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא presses the contradiction against רב חסדא, which has not been answered yet. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסח case, רב חסדא treats the ערל as fit because he could circumcise, which is really a הואיל argument. In the baking case he says we do not say הואיל. So his two rulings seem to clash.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא דְּרַב חִסְדָּא אַדְּרַב חִסְדָּא קַשְׁיָא!
phrases.english: But Rav Chisda against Rav Chisda is difficult!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא דְּרַב חִסְדָּא אַדְּרַב חִסְדָּא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with step 6: רבה is fine, but רב חסדא remains difficult.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: He uses 'he could circumcise' (a הואיל idea) for the פסח, but rejects הואיל for the baker.

steps.title: רב חסדא uses הואיל only to be strict
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא rejects הואיל when it would make things easier, such as exempting from מלקות. He accepts it when it makes things stricter, such as disqualifying the פסח.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: when רב חסדא does not accept 'since,' that is to be lenient. To be strict, he does accept it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction against רב חסדא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the baking case, הואיל would make things easier by removing מלקות, so רב חסדא does not use it. In the פסח case, treating the ערל as בר כפרה makes things stricter, because intent for him can now make the קרבן פסול. So רב חסדא uses הואיל there.

keyTerms.meaning: Since; treating what could happen as if it already applies

steps.whatToRemember: רבה: הואיל works unless an action is missing. רב חסדא: הואיל is used only to be strict.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרִי: כִּי לֵית לֵיהּ לְרַב חִסְדָּא ״הוֹאִיל״ — לְקוּלָּא,
phrases.english: They say: when Rav Chisda does not hold of 'since', it is to be lenient;
to be strict, he does hold of it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: כִּי לֵית לֵיהּ לְרַב חִסְדָּא הוֹאִיל
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the principle to strict vs. lenient outcomes
steps.terutzMaskana: He rejects it only for leniency, and applies it for stringency.

steps.title: מר זוטרא quotes a ברייתא comparing ערלה to טומאה
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא quotes a ברייתא. Both ערלה and טומאה disqualify a פסח. Just as partial טומאה is not treated like full טומאה, partial ערלה is not treated like full ערלה.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא, son of רב מרי, said to רבינא: It is taught: since ערלה disqualifies and טומאה disqualifies, then just as with טומאה partial impurity was not made like full impurity, so too with ערלה partial ערלה was not made like full ערלה.
steps.whatsHappening: A new discussion opens. מר זוטרא quotes a ברייתא to set up a question about what kind of טומאה it means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא learns the rule for ערלה from the rule for טומאה. To understand this comparison, we need to know which kind of 'partial טומאה' the ברייתא has in mind. The next steps ask exactly that.

keyTerms.meaning: Like all of it / like the whole

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב מָרִי לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Mar Zutra son of Rav Mari said to Ravina:
It is taught: since lack of circumcision disqualifies
and impurity disqualifies,
just as with impurity, [the Torah] did not make
partial impurity like full impurity,
so too with lack of circumcision, it did not make
partial uncircumcision like full uncircumcision.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב מָרִי לְרָבִינָא: קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: understanding a ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Partial ערלה does not disqualify like full ערלה, learned from טומאה.

steps.title: Which kind of impurity? First suggestion: impure people
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'טומאה' means here. It first suggests impure people: some impure people in the group do not disqualify the pure ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: This impurity, what case is it? If you say it is impurity of people, then 'partial impurity is not like full impurity' means: if there are four or five impure men and four or five pure men, the impure ones do not disqualify the pure ones.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what kind of טומאה the ברייתא means and tries a first answer. This answer is set up to be knocked down next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first suggestion is that 'partial טומאה' means a group that is partly impure. On this reading, the impure members do not ruin the פסח for the pure members.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (a suggestion that will be rejected)

phrases.english: This impurity, what are the circumstances?
If you say it is the impurity of people,

phrases.aramaic: וּמַאי ״לֹא עָשָׂה בָּהּ מִקְצָת טוּמְאָה כְּכׇל טוּמְאָה״ —
phrases.english: and what is 'partial impurity was not made like full impurity'?

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִי אִיכָּא אַרְבְּעָה וְחַמְשָׁה גַּבְרֵי טְמֵאִין
phrases.english: that if there are four or five impure men
and four or five pure men,
the impure do not disqualify the pure,

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי טוּמְאָה הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִילֵּימָא בְּטוּמְאַת גַּבְרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of the ברייתא quoted in step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of טומאה the ברייתא is talking about.

steps.title: Impure people can't be meant, since ערלים in a group are already clearly fine
steps.stepSummary: A משנה already says a פסח slaughtered for both circumcised and uncircumcised people is כשר. So there would be nothing to learn about ערלה. Why would the ברייתא be unsure about ערלה but sure about טומאה?
steps.simpleTranslation: With ערלה too, they do not disqualify, as we learned: for circumcised and uncircumcised, it is valid. So what is different about טומאה, which is obvious to him, and what is different about ערלה, which he is unsure about?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the first suggestion from step 10.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'partial' means a mixed group, then the ערלה rule is already stated openly in a משנה, just like the טומאה rule. Then the two cases are exactly the same, so the ברייתא would have no reason to be unsure about ערלה and need to learn it from טומאה.

phrases.aramaic: גַּבֵּי עׇרְלָה נָמֵי הָא לָא פָּסְלִי,
phrases.english: With regard to lack of circumcision too, they do not disqualify,
as we learned: for circumcised and uncircumcised, it is valid.
What is different about impurity, that it is obvious to him,
and what is different about lack of circumcision, that he is in doubt?

steps.triggerLanguage: גַּבֵּי עׇרְלָה נָמֵי הָא לָא פָּסְלִי, דִּתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the 'impure people' reading from step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The reading of טומאה as impure people
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Under that reading, the ערלה case would be just as obvious as טומאה, so the comparison would be pointless.

steps.title: It means impurity of the meat
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא means impure meat. If one limb becomes impure, we burn that limb and still eat the rest.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is impurity of the meat. And what is 'partial impurity was not made like full impurity'? If one of the limbs became impure, the one that became impure we burn, and the rest we eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the correct reading: the ברייתא is talking about the meat of the פסח becoming partly impure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here 'partial טומאה' means only part of the meat is impure. The impure part is burned, but the rest of the פסח is still eaten. The ברייתא then compares 'partial ערלה' to this kind of case.
steps.whatToRemember: The טומאה in the ברייתא is impurity of the meat: if part of the meat is impure, only that part is burned, and the rest is eaten.

phrases.english: Rather, it is impurity of the meat,

phrases.aramaic: וּמַאי לֹא עָשָׂה בָּהּ מִקְצָת טוּמְאָה כְּכׇל טוּמְאָה?
phrases.english: and what is 'partial impurity was not made like full impurity'?
that if one of the limbs became impure,
the one that became impure, we burn it,
and the rest, we eat it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected reading from steps 10-11 with a new one.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא's טומאה is impurity of the meat: the impure limb is burned and the rest is eaten.

steps.title: The second half of the ברייתא does not fit 'impure meat'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the reading from step 12 using the סיפא. The סיפא says טומאה 'does not apply to all offerings,' but impure meat matters for every offering.
steps.simpleTranslation: How did you explain the ברייתא? As impure meat? Then read the end of it: 'We learn something that does not apply to all offerings from something else that does not apply to all offerings. And do not bring proof from wrong-time intent, which applies to all offerings.' Now, what טומאה is meant here? If it is impure meat, why does it say it does not apply to all offerings?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the answer from step 12, that טומאה means impure meat. It reads the next line of the same ברייתא to show that this answer causes a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סיפא explains why ערלה is compared to טומאה and not to wrong-time intent (פיגול). The reason given is that ערלה and טומאה are alike: neither one 'applies to all offerings.' But impure meat is a problem for every offering, so the reading from step 12 does not fit this line.

keyTerms.meaning: How did you set up (explain) the case?
The later part (end) of a משנה or ברייתא
We derive / learn one law from another
Let it not prove (do not bring a proof from it)
Intent to eat the offering outside its allowed time (פיגול-type thought)

steps.confusionAlert: 'Does not apply to all offerings' is not about which offerings become impure. It describes a special feature that ערלה and טומאה share with each other, which time-intent does not share.

phrases.english: How did you set it up? As impurity of the meat?
phrases.notes: Points back to the answer in step 12.

phrases.english: Say (read) the latter clause:

phrases.aramaic: דָּנִין דָּבָר שֶׁאֵינוֹ נוֹהֵג בְּכׇל הַזְּבָחִים
phrases.english: We derive a matter that does not apply to all offerings
from a matter that does not apply to all offerings,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַל יוֹכִיחַ זְמַן שֶׁנּוֹהֵג בְּכׇל הַזְּבָחִים.
phrases.english: and let 'time' (wrong-time intent), which applies to all offerings, not prove anything.
And what impurity is meant?
If we say impurity of the meat,
why does it not apply to all offerings?
phrases.notes: Impure meat is a problem for every offering.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמַאי אוֹקֵימְתָּא — בְּטוּמְאַת בָּשָׂר? אֵימָא סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 12 using the next line of the same ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of טומאה as impure meat (step 12).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The סיפא says טומאה does not apply to all offerings. Impure meat applies to every offering, so the reading from step 12 contradicts the סיפא.

steps.title: So the second half must mean impure people, and the two halves no longer match
steps.stepSummary: The סיפא only makes sense if it means impure people. People who are impure or uncircumcised can send other offerings, but not a פסח. That leaves the first half about meat and the second half about people.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is obvious that it means impure people. And what does 'does not apply to all offerings' mean? For all other offerings, an uncircumcised or impure person may send his offering. But for the פסח, an uncircumcised or impure person may not send his פסח. So the first half is about impure meat and the second half is about impure people!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the סיפא only works if it means impure people. Then it points out that this splits the ברייתא into two different meanings of טומאה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With any other offering, an impure person or a ערל can still have it brought for him, even though he cannot eat it. A פסח cannot be brought for such a person. So 'impure people' really is a rule that does not apply to all offerings. But then the רישא (impure meat) and the סיפא (impure people) use the same word in two different ways, and that is the difficulty.

keyTerms.meaning: Impurity of the people (the eaters), not of the meat
They send their offerings (to be brought for them)
The first part of a משנה or ברייתא

phrases.english: Rather, it is obvious: impurity of the people,
and what is 'does not apply to all offerings'?
That with all other offerings —
an uncircumcised man and an impure man send their offerings,
whereas with the פסח —
an uncircumcised man and an impure man do not send their פסח offerings.
The first clause is about impure meat
phrases.notes: This was the answer of step 12.

phrases.english: and the latter clause is about impure people!
phrases.notes: The גמרא is raising a difficulty here.

steps.triggerLanguage: רֵישָׁא בְּטוּמְאַת בָּשָׂר וְסֵיפָא בְּטוּמְאַת גַּבְרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the challenge of step 13 by showing its forced result: two meanings of טומאה in one ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: How consistent the ברייתא's use of the word טומאה is.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One ברייתא should not use the same word to mean impure meat in the first half and impure people in the second half.

steps.title: Yes, the ברייתא argues from the general name 'טומאה'
steps.stepSummary: The answer accepts the split. The ברייתא is using the general category 'טומאה,' so each half can point to a different kind of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Yes. He is arguing from the name 'טומאה.'
steps.whatsHappening: The challenge is accepted instead of pushed away. Yes, the two halves refer to different kinds of טומאה, and that is fine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is not tied to one specific kind of impurity. It reasons from the general idea of טומאה. One kind fits the first point (partial impurity does not ruin the whole), and the other kind fits the second point (it does not apply to all offerings).

keyTerms.meaning: The general name / category of impurity
He is arguing / drawing his comparison

phrases.english: He said to him: Yes,
phrases.notes: רבינא said this to מר זוטרא.

phrases.english: he argues from the name 'impurity.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִין, שֵׁם טוּמְאָה קָא פָרֵיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 13-14 by accepting that the two halves differ.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepting the difficulty: the general category of טומאה covers both meanings.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A single ברייתא must use טומאה in one consistent sense.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא reasons from the general category 'טומאה,' so it can use different kinds of it in each half.

steps.title: Second answer: the second half is also about impure meat
steps.stepSummary: A second answer keeps both halves about impure meat. 'Does not apply to all offerings' means that for other offerings, the blood is still sprinkled even if only the fats or only the meat stays pure.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or if you want, say: the latter clause is also about impure meat. And what does 'does not apply to all offerings' mean? For all other offerings, whether the fats became impure and the meat is still there, or the meat became impure and the fats are still there, the כהן sprinkles the blood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer. It keeps the whole ברייתא about impure meat by explaining 'not for all offerings' in a new way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With other offerings, it is enough that either the fats (for the altar) or the meat (for eating) stays pure, and the blood may still be sprinkled. The implied contrast is the פסח, which is mainly for eating, so impure meat affects it differently. So impure meat really does have a rule that 'does not apply to all offerings,' and the two halves now match.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces another answer)
The fats of an offering that are burned on the altar
He sprinkles the blood on the altar

steps.whatToRemember: Two answers: (1) the ברייתא argues from the general category טומאה, so the halves can differ; (2) both halves are about impure meat, and other offerings stay valid if either the fats or the meat remain pure.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
The latter clause is also about impurity of the meat.
And what is 'it does not apply to all offerings'?
That with all other offerings,
whether the fats became impure and the meat remains,
or the meat became impure and the fats remain —
he sprinkles the blood.
phrases.notes: Either part being pure is enough for other offerings, unlike the פסח.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: סֵיפָא נָמֵי בְּטוּמְאַת בָּשָׂר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the same challenge, keeping the ברייתא consistent.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the phrase 'does not apply to all offerings.'
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Impure meat matters the same way for every offering, so the סיפא cannot be about meat.
steps.terutzMaskana: For other offerings, the blood may be sprinkled if either the fats or the meat remain pure. The פסח is different, so impure meat is indeed a rule that does not apply to all offerings.

steps.title: With a פסח, the meat must stay pure for the blood to be sprinkled
steps.stepSummary: This finishes the second answer. With a פסח, if only the fats became impure, the blood is still sprinkled. If the meat became impure, the blood is not sprinkled, even when the fats are still pure.
steps.simpleTranslation: But with a פסח: if the fats became impure and the meat is still pure, he sprinkles the blood. If the meat became impure and the fats are still pure, he does not sprinkle the blood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא completes the answer from step 16 by showing how the פסח is different from all other offerings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For other offerings, it is enough for either the fats or the meat to stay pure. For a פסח, only pure meat makes the offering work, because eating the פסח is its main purpose. So 'טומאה does not apply to all offerings' can still be about impure meat: the meat rule is stricter only for the פסח.

keyTerms.meaning: The fats of an offering that are burned on the מזבח
He sprinkles the blood on the מזבח, the key act that makes the offering valid

steps.whatToRemember: Other offerings: pure fats OR pure meat is enough to sprinkle the blood. פסח: the meat must stay pure, because eating it is the main point.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not reverse the two cases. Impure fats with pure meat means the blood is sprinkled. Impure meat with pure fats means the blood is not sprinkled.
steps.whyThisMatters: This contrast is what lets the second answer read the whole ברייתא as being about impure meat.

phrases.english: But with the Paschal offering,
if the fats became impure and the meat remains pure
he sprinkles the blood;
if the meat became impure and the fats remain pure
he does not sprinkle the blood.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the second answer begun in step 16 by stating the פסח side of the contrast.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefinition of the סיפא: 'not in all offerings' means the meat rule is stricter for the פסח than for other offerings.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Impure meat matters equally for every offering, so the סיפא could not be about meat.
steps.terutzMaskana: Impure meat does not stop the blood in other offerings if the fats are pure, but it does stop the blood in a פסח.

steps.title: Challenge from the last clause: impurity was permitted from its rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the reading that the ברייתא is about impure meat. The סיפא says that טומאה cannot be used as a counter-proof because it 'was permitted from its rule.'
steps.simpleTranslation: How did you explain the ברייתא? As impure meat? Then look at the last part: 'We learn a rule that was never relaxed from another rule that was never relaxed. And טומאה cannot be brought as a counter-proof, because it was relaxed in some cases.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the 'impure meat' reading by quoting a different line from the end of the same ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סיפא learns the law of ערלה from another strict law that never has exceptions: wrong-time intent (זמן). It rejects טומאה as a comparison because טומאה has an exception: when most of the community is impure, a פסח may be brought in טומאה. The question is whether that exception fits impure meat, or only impure people.

keyTerms.meaning: How did you establish it? (asks what case you set the source in)
Say the last part (of the same source)
We derive, we learn one law from another
Was never permitted from its general rule; has no exceptions
Do not bring it as a counter-proof

steps.confusionAlert: 'Permitted from its rule' does not mean טומאה is allowed in general. It means the strict rule has a known exception, such as a community that is mostly impure.

phrases.english: How did you establish it?
As impurity of the meat?
Say the last clause:
We derive a matter that was never permitted from its rule
from a matter that was never permitted from its rule,
and let impurity not serve as a counter-proof,
since it was permitted from its rule.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמַאי אוֹקֵימְתָּא בְּטוּמְאַת בָּשָׂר אֵימָא סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the 'impure meat' reading, which steps 12, 16 and 17 rely on, using another clause of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the ברייתא's טומאה means impure meat.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The סיפא describes טומאה as having an exception. The גמרא will test whether that exception can apply to impure meat.

steps.title: Which kind of impurity does this clause mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to ask which kind of טומאה the סיפא means, starting with 'if you say.' This passage ends in the middle of the sentence.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what kind of טומאה is this speaking? If you say...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It is about to try out each kind of טומאה to see which one fits the words 'permitted from its rule.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'אילימא' signals that the גמרא will suggest one option and then knock it down. Most likely it will test impure meat first, and ask whether impure meat was ever permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say... (introduces a suggestion that will usually be rejected)

phrases.english: About what?
If you say...

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets up the detailed analysis of the קשיא from step 18 by asking which kind of טומאה fits the סיפא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which type of טומאה (impure meat or impure people) is meant by 'טומאה was permitted from its rule.'
